headline: State desk: Georgia plans e-cards; Florida flower nears 200M grams
dek: Georgia proposed medical cannabis rules on 20 November with a hearing on 8 December; Florida's 20 November report shows 795 stores and 943,221 patients.
key_points: Georgia's Department of Public Health proposed rules on 20 November that would let patients use an electronic registration card and buy without waiting for a physical one.
Georgia will hold an online hearing on 8 December, take written comments until 9 December and consider adoption around 18 December.
Florida's 20 November state report counts 943,221 patients and 795 dispensing locations, with 150,691 ounces of smokable flower sold in the week to 19 November.
Trulieve sold 33.1% of Florida's flower that week from 172 of the 795 stores; flower bought per patient this year is up about 6%.
body: Two southern medical markets moved this week in ways that matter to operators. Georgia published draft rules that would remove a waiting step for new patients. Florida's weekly state report showed sales still growing several times faster than the patient count, with four more stores approved.
Both are medical-only states. Neither has adult-use sales. That makes patient access rules and store counts the main levers on revenue.
## Georgia: buy on approval, not on delivery of a card

Georgia's Department of Public Health published a notice of proposed rulemaking on Friday 20 November to update Chapter 511-5-11 of the state's regulations, according to The Marijuana Herald, which reviewed the notice. The changes implement Senate Bill 220, the Putting Georgia's Patients First Act, which Governor Brian Kemp signed in May and which took effect on 1 July.

The headline change is the card. Patients and caregivers could choose a physical registration card, an electronic one, or both. An electronic card would let a patient buy as soon as the state has received an eligible application, without waiting for plastic to arrive in the post. There is a condition: the Herald reports that electronic cards depend on the legislature funding them.

The draft also writes several parts of SB 220 into rule. Registration cards would be valid for five years. Most patients would still need a physician to certify each year that they have a qualifying condition; patients with incurable or irreversible conditions would be exempt from the yearly step. A physician's failure to file a required annual report would not, on its own, let the department cancel a patient's or caregiver's card.

Two further changes widen who can take part. The definition of caregiver would cover adults a patient designates to help obtain and administer the medicine, and health care institutions that agree to let patients possess and use it on their premises. On records, police and prosecutors could ask the department to verify whether a person is registered, and the Georgia Composite Medical Board could receive registry information for investigations and discipline.
## Why it matters for Georgia operators

Georgia's market is small and young, and SB 220 rebuilt it. The law replaced the old low-THC oil framework, widened eligibility for several conditions and raised the possession limit to products containing a combined 12,000 milligrams of THC, according to the Herald.

Every day between a doctor's certification and a first purchase is a day of lost sales, and some patients never complete the trip. An electronic card closes that gap. The institutional caregiver language matters for a different reason: it opens a route into hospices and care homes, where patients cannot easily travel to a dispensary. As we reported on 17 November, a Georgia licensee has already begun shipping medical cannabis to patients' homes.
The funding condition is the weak point. A rule that allows electronic cards does nothing until money is appropriated to issue them. We flag that the draft, as described, sets no date for that.
> Georgia is cutting the wait between approval and first purchase. Florida shows what happens when the stores are already there.
## Florida: sales outrun patients again
Florida's Office of Medical Marijuana Use published its weekly update on 20 November. We read the report. It counts 943,221 qualified patients with active cards and 795 approved dispensing locations.

In the week of 13 to 19 November, treatment centres dispensed 150,691 ounces of marijuana in a form for smoking and 452.5 million milligrams of THC in other products. The Herald's comparison with the same week of 2025 puts flower up 7.4% and other THC products up 9.1%.

For the year to 19 November, the Herald's tally of the state data is about 193.66 million grams of flower, up 7.8% on the same period of 2025, and 19.83 billion milligrams of THC in other forms, up 8.2%. The patient count rose 1.4% over the same period, from 929,916. Dividing one by the other, flower bought per patient is about 205 grams this year against about 193 grams last year, a rise of roughly 6%. Growth is coming from existing patients buying more, not from new ones.
## Who is selling it
The report lists dispensations by licence holder. Our calculations from that table for the latest week:

Trulieve dispensed 49,891 ounces of flower from 172 locations, which is 33.1% of the state total from 21.6% of the stores. Curaleaf dispensed 17,630 ounces from 82 locations, or 11.7%. Verano's MÜV dispensed 16,544 ounces from 89 locations, or 11.0%. Green Dragon dispensed 11,447 ounces from 74 locations, or 7.6%. Together those four account for 63% of flower and 417 of the 795 stores.
Trulieve's share is down from close to 35% in the report we covered on 14 November. One week does not make a trend, but it is the figure to track as rivals add stores.

Store count is not the same as store strength. The state average was about 190 ounces of flower per location for the week. Trulieve averaged about 290. Jungle Boys, with 15 locations, averaged about 371, the highest of any operator with more than a handful of stores.

The department approved four new locations during the week: Curaleaf in Sebring and North Fort Myers, MÜV in Tarpon Springs and Trulieve in Haines City. The Herald puts the store count a year ago at 734, so the network has grown by 61 locations, or 8.3%, in twelve months, almost exactly in line with sales volume. As we reported on 19 November, operators have been opening stores ahead of the Thanksgiving week.
## What to watch

In Georgia, watch the online public hearing on 8 December at 2 p.m. Eastern, the close of written comments on 9 December, and the department's adoption decision expected around 18 December. Then watch whether the 2027 budget funds electronic cards. In Florida, watch next week's report for Thanksgiving-week volume, usually among the strongest of the year, and for whether Trulieve's share of flower holds above a third as the store count passes 800.
